note: The backend-owned text of the showcase page's stepper and code walk for this backend: per block type its stage kind, words, formula, prose, recompute and code anchor; per activation its curve and bend; per link its formula and answer rule; and the fixed walk steps. vega-show copies the subset a lane uses into page.json. Prose follows the digit rule: no digit outside a placeholder. tests/test_explain_catalog_sync.py keeps it in step with coverage.json, the catalog, the blocks and the page's walk.

placeholders.units: the stage's output width: its units, outputs or numbers per position
placeholders.inputs: the stage's input width: the numbers each unit reads
placeholders.layers: the stacked layers of an encoder or a recurrent block
placeholders.n_sub: the input width written as a subscript, for the last term of a sum
placeholders.slope: the negative slope of a LeakyReLU, the activation's or the graph attention's
placeholders.eps: the small constant added under a square root
placeholders.v: the letter of the stage's input: x for the shaped inputs, a for the outputs of the layer before

weighted_sum.what: one unit's weighted sum of its inputs plus its bias, then its activation

cumulative_score.what: the ordinal head's shared score plus each ordered threshold

elementwise.what: the activation applied to each number on its own

lookup.what: the table row a nominal value picks

batchnorm.what: each unit shifted and rescaled with the running statistics fitted in training

layernorm.what: the vector centred and scaled by its own mean and spread, then each unit's gain and shift

residual_sum.what: the block's input, projected when the widths differ, plus what its inner layers computed

branch_merge.what: the branches' outputs laid side by side, or added

conv1d.what: one output channel at one position from the kernel, the bias and the input under the window

pool1d.what: one pooled value: the maximum or the mean of its group of positions

rnn_step.what: one step of one unit: the bent sum of the input and the previous state

gru_step.what: one step of one unit: the reset and update gates, the candidate and the new state

lstm_step.what: one step of one unit: the input, forget and output gates, the candidate, the cell and the output

attention_row.what: one query position's attention weights and its weighted mix of the values

attention_pool.what: the step weights from the score and query layers, and the weighted sum of the states

transformer_layer.what: one encoder layer: the attention part and the feed-forward part, each added back

token_affine.what: one input's token from its learned vector and bias, or its table row

pool_reduce.what: the mean, the maximum or the first position over the sequence

latent_mean.what: the mean half of the input, which is the code while answering

gcn_message.what: one node's sum of its neighbours' projected vectors times their normalised coefficients, plus the bias

sage_message.what: one node's own projection plus the projection of its neighbours' aggregate

gat_message.what: one node's attention coefficients per head and the weighted sum of its neighbours

gin_message.what: one node's scaled own vector plus its neighbours' sum, through the small network

graph_readout.what: the sum, mean or maximum over one graph's nodes

none.what: nothing is recomputed: the formula and the shapes only

dense.label: dense layer
dense.formula: z = w₁·{v}₁ + w₂·{v}₂ + … + w{n_sub}·{v}{n_sub} + b ; a = f(z)
dense.prose: Each of the {units} units of this layer adds up the {inputs} numbers it receives, each times a weight of its own, plus a bias; then its activation, if it has one, bends the sum:
dense.unit_how: A unit takes every number of the layer before it, multiplies each by a weight of its own, and adds them up with one more number, its bias. Then the activation bends the sum; without that bend, all the layers together would be no more than one weighted sum.

walk.title: A dense layer: z = W·x + b
walk.text: One matrix product plus a bias. W is the grid of weights the network page draws as edges; one row of it times the inputs, plus one bias, is the z that the stepper adds up term by term.

embedding.label: embedding
embedding.prose: Each nominal {feature.one} has a table of its own, one row per value it took in training: the value picks its row, a short list of learned numbers, and the rows of every nominal {feature.one} are laid side by side. A value never seen in training takes the table's reserved last row.
embedding.unit_how: An embedding does no arithmetic: it looks a value up and hands on the row of learned numbers that stands for it, so values that act alike end up with rows that look alike.

walk.title: Nominal values as learned numbers
walk.text: One table per nominal {feature.one}, each row a short vector the training moved like any other weight. The id the recipe gave the value picks the row, and the recipe's reserved id for unseen values picks the last one, so a new value is answered rather than refused.

concat.label: join
concat.prose: The numeric inputs and every embedding row are laid side by side into one list of numbers; nothing is computed.
concat.unit_how: A join computes nothing: it places the numeric inputs and the embedded nominal ones side by side, so the next layer reads them all as one list.

walk.title: Numbers and embeddings, side by side
walk.text: The numeric inputs and the embedding rows are joined into one list, the width the next layer reads: the numeric {feature.many} first, then the row of each nominal {feature.one} in the contract's order.

batchnorm.label: batch normalisation
batchnorm.prose: While answering, each of the {units} units is shifted and rescaled with numbers fitted in training: μ and σ² are the running mean and variance it saw, γ and β its learned gain and shift, and ε = {eps} keeps the division safe:
batchnorm.unit_how: A normalised unit subtracts the mean it saw in training, divides by the spread it saw, and then applies a learned gain and shift, so the next layer always reads numbers on a familiar scale.

walk.title: Batch normalisation, frozen for answering
walk.text: In training this layer measured the mean and variance of each unit over each batch and kept running averages of them. While answering it uses only those running values, so the answer for a {row.one} never depends on the other {row.many} of the request.

layernorm.label: layer normalisation
layernorm.prose: Each vector of {units} numbers is centred on its own mean and divided by its own spread, with ε = {eps} under the square root; then each unit applies its learned gain γ and shift β:
layernorm.unit_how: A layer normalisation looks at one vector at a time: it centres its numbers on their mean, scales them by their spread, and lets each unit apply a learned gain and shift. Nothing is fitted across {row.many}.

walk.title: Layer normalisation
walk.text: The numbers of one vector are centred and scaled by their own mean and spread, with nothing fitted across {row.many}; then each unit's learned gain and shift are applied.

dropout.label: dropout
dropout.formula: training: y = m ⊙ x / (1 − p) ; answering: y = x
dropout.prose: While the network trained, this step silenced each number with probability p = {p:pct} and scaled the others up to make up for them. While it answers, it does nothing: every number passes unchanged.
dropout.unit_how: Dropout only acts in training, where it silences a random share of the numbers so that no unit can lean on another. While answering it passes everything through, so the same {row.one} always gets the same answer.

walk.title: Dropout, off while answering
walk.text: While the network trains, dropout silences a random share of units so that none can lean on another. While it answers, it does nothing: the predictor puts the model in evaluation mode, so the same {row.one} always gets the same answer.

activation.label: activation
activation.prose: Each of the {units} numbers is bent by the same function, one at a time:
activation.unit_how: An activation bends each number on its own by a fixed function; without it, the layers around it would multiply out into a single weighted sum.

walk.title: The non-linearity
walk.text: A function chosen by name from a table in this file bends each z. Without it the layers would multiply out into a single matrix — that single matrix is the effective linear reading the page gives for a unit, and the bend is why that reading is only an approximation.

residual.label: residual block
residual.formula: y = x + f(x) ; with a projection: y = P·x + f(x)
residual.prose: The inner layers compute f(x) from the block's input x, and the block adds their result to x itself; when the widths differ, a learned projection P brings x to the new width first:
residual.unit_how: A residual block lets its input skip over the inner layers and adds it to what they computed, so the inner layers only have to learn a correction.

walk.title: A residual block: x + f(x)
walk.text: The inner layers run as usual, and their output is added to the block's own input. When the inner layers change the width, a learned projection brings the input to the new width before the addition. Each repeat of the block starts from what the one before it produced.

sequential.label: block sequence
sequential.prose: The inner blocks run one after the other, each one's output the next one's input.
sequential.unit_how: A sequence of blocks computes nothing of its own: it runs its inner blocks in order.

walk.title: Blocks in sequence
walk.text: A group of blocks run in order, each one's output the next one's input; the group only gives them a shared place in the spec.

parallel.label: parallel block
parallel.formula: y = [f₁(x) ‖ … ‖ fₖ(x)] or y = Σᵢ fᵢ(x)
parallel.prose: Every branch reads the same input; their outputs are then laid side by side, or added when the merge is a sum:
parallel.unit_how: Parallel branches each read the same input and compute their own view of it; the block keeps all of them, side by side or added together.

walk.title: Parallel branches
walk.text: Every branch reads the same input, and the block merges what they computed: side by side when the merge is concat, added element by element when it is sum.

conv1d.label: convolution
conv1d.formula: y[c′, t] = b[c′] + Σ_c Σ_(j < {kernel}) W[c′, c, j] · x[c, t·s + j − pad]
conv1d.prose: Each of the {channels} output channels slides a window of {kernel} {step.many} along the sequence: at every position it multiplies the numbers under the window by its weights, adds them up across every input channel, and adds its bias:
conv1d.unit_how: A convolution channel is a small pattern detector: it slides along the {step.many} of the {window.one}, and at each position it adds up the numbers under it, each times a weight of its own, plus a bias.

walk.title: A convolution along the {step.many}
walk.text: The same small set of weights is applied at every position of the {window.one}, so a pattern is recognised wherever it occurs. The channel axis is moved in and out around the convolution, so every other block keeps reading {step.many} first and channels last.

pool1d.label: pooling layer
pool1d.formula: y[c, t] = max_(j < size) x[c, t·size + j] (or the mean)
pool1d.prose: The sequence is cut into consecutive groups of {step.many}, and each channel keeps the largest number of each group, or their mean:
pool1d.unit_how: A pooling layer shortens the sequence: each group of neighbouring {step.many} becomes one, holding the largest value of the group or its mean, channel by channel.

walk.title: Pooling along the {step.many}
walk.text: Neighbouring {step.many} are merged group by group, keeping the maximum or the mean of each channel, so the layers after it read a shorter sequence.

rnn.label: recurrent layer
rnn.formula: hₜ = tanh(W_ih·xₜ + b_ih + W_hh·hₜ₋₁ + b_hh) (ReLU in place of tanh when chosen)
rnn.prose: The layer reads the {window.one} one {step.one} at a time and carries a state of {hidden} numbers from each {step.one} to the next: the new state is the bent sum of this {step.one}'s inputs and the previous state, each through weights of their own:
rnn.unit_how: A recurrent unit keeps a memory of what it has read so far: at each {step.one} it mixes the new inputs with its previous state and bends the result into its new state.

walk.title: A recurrent layer
walk.text: The layer walks the {window.one} {step.one} by {step.one}, carrying a state forward; what the next block receives is the state after the last {step.one}, every state, or their mean or maximum, as the spec's return option says. With two directions, a second pass reads the {window.one} backwards and the two states are laid side by side.

gru.label: GRU layer
gru.formula: r = σ(W_ir·x + b_ir + W_hr·h + b_hr) ; z = σ(W_iz·x + b_iz + W_hz·h + b_hz) ; n = tanh(W_in·x + b_in + r ⊙ (W_hn·h + b_hn)) ; h′ = (1 − z) ⊙ n + z ⊙ h
gru.prose: At each {step.one} the GRU computes two gates from the inputs and its previous state of {hidden} numbers: r decides how much of the old state feeds the candidate n, and z how much of the old state is kept rather than replaced by n:
gru.unit_how: A GRU unit keeps a memory and, at each {step.one}, decides with two gates how much of it to reset and how much to overwrite with a new candidate computed from the inputs.

walk.title: A GRU layer
walk.text: PyTorch's gated recurrent unit, its gates in PyTorch's order: reset r, update z, candidate n. The state after each {step.one} blends the old state and the candidate by the update gate; the spec's return option picks what the next block reads.

lstm.label: LSTM layer
lstm.formula: i = σ(W_ii·x + b_ii + W_hi·h + b_hi) ; f = σ(W_if·x + b_if + W_hf·h + b_hf) ; g = tanh(W_ig·x + b_ig + W_hg·h + b_hg) ; o = σ(W_io·x + b_io + W_ho·h + b_ho) ; c′ = f ⊙ c + i ⊙ g ; h′ = o ⊙ tanh(c′)
lstm.prose: At each {step.one} the LSTM computes three gates and a candidate from the inputs and its previous output of {hidden} numbers: f decides what the cell keeps, i what it takes from the candidate g, and o what it shows as its new output:
lstm.unit_how: An LSTM unit carries a cell, a memory guarded by gates: at each {step.one} it forgets part of the cell, writes part of a new candidate into it, and shows a gated view of the cell as its output.

walk.title: An LSTM layer
walk.text: PyTorch's long short-term memory, its gates in PyTorch's order: input i, forget f, candidate g, output o. The cell c carries the memory across {step.many}, and the output h is what the next {step.one}, and finally the next block, reads.

attention.label: attention layer
attention.formula: Q, K, V = x·W_q + b_q, x·W_k + b_k, x·W_v + b_v ; A = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_h) per head ; y = [A₁V₁ ‖ … ‖ A_hV_h]·W_o + b_o (the mean over the positions when pooled)
attention.prose: Each of the {heads} heads compares every position with every other through learned queries Q and keys K, turns the similarities into weights that add up to one, and mixes the values V with them; the heads' results are joined and projected back:
attention.unit_how: An attention layer lets every position look at every other: it scores how relevant each one is, turns the scores into weights, and takes the weighted mix of what the positions carry.

walk.title: Self-attention
walk.text: Queries, keys and values are three projections of the same input. Each head weighs every position by how well its key matches the query, and the weighted values of all heads are joined and projected back to the input's width. With pooling on, the positions are then averaged into one vector.

attention_pool.label: attention pooling
attention_pool.formula: α = softmaxₜ(q · tanh(W·hₜ + b)) ; y = Σₜ αₜ·hₜ
attention_pool.prose: One learned query weighs the {step.many}: each {step.one}'s state hₜ is scored through a small tanh layer, the scores become weights αₜ that add up to one, and the output is the states' weighted sum:
attention_pool.unit_how: Attention pooling reads a whole sequence of states and keeps one: a weighted mix in which the {step.many} the learned query finds most relevant weigh most.

walk.title: Attention pooling
walk.text: A learned query scores each {step.one}'s state through a small tanh layer, a softmax over the {step.many} turns the scores into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the states. The weights say which {step.many} the answer leaned on; the inspector recomputes them from the score and query layers rather than keeping them.

transformer_encoder.label: transformer encoder
transformer_encoder.formula: per layer, normalisation first: x ← x + MHA(LN₁(x)) ; x ← x + W₂·ReLU(W₁·LN₂(x) + b₁) + b₂
transformer_encoder.prose: Each of the {layers} encoder layers first lets every token attend to every other through {heads} heads, then passes each token through a small feed-forward network; both parts read a normalised copy of the tokens and add their result back to them:
transformer_encoder.unit_how: An encoder layer mixes information between tokens with attention, then processes each token on its own with a small feed-forward network; each part adds its result to what came in.

walk.title: A transformer encoder
walk.text: PyTorch's encoder layers with the normalisation first: every token is normalised before the attention and before the feed-forward part, and each part's result is added back to the token. The layers are stacked, each reading the tokens the one before it wrote.

feature_tokenizer.label: feature tokenizer
feature_tokenizer.formula: t₀ = [cls] ; tⱼ = xⱼ·wⱼ + bⱼ for a numeric input ; tₖ = Eₖ[idₖ] for a nominal one
feature_tokenizer.prose: Every input becomes a token of {units} numbers: a numeric {feature.one} scales a learned vector of its own and adds a bias of its own, a nominal one looks its value up in a table of its own, and a learned [cls] token is put first:
feature_tokenizer.unit_how: A tokenizer turns each input into a small vector of its own, so that the attention layers after it can compare the inputs with each other.

walk.title: Inputs to tokens
walk.text: Each numeric {feature.one} multiplies a learned vector and adds a learned bias; each nominal one picks a row of its own table. A learned [cls] token goes first, and a pooling step later may read it alone.

positional.label: positional encoding
positional.prose: Each position t gets its own vector PE[t] added, sinusoidal or learned, so the layers after it can tell the positions apart.
positional.unit_how: A positional encoding adds to each position a vector that says where it stands, since attention by itself does not know the order.

walk.title: Where each position stands
walk.text: Attention compares positions without knowing their order, so a vector that encodes the position is added to each one: fixed sine and cosine waves, or learned numbers, as the spec says.

flatten.label: flatten
flatten.prose: The positions and their channels are laid end to end into one long list of numbers; nothing is computed.
flatten.unit_how: Flattening computes nothing: it lays a sequence of vectors end to end so a dense layer can read them all.

walk.title: Flatten
walk.text: The sequence of vectors is laid end to end as one long list, so the dense layers after it see every position at once.

reshape.label: reshape
reshape.prose: The numbers are rearranged into the shape the next block reads; nothing is computed.
reshape.unit_how: A reshape computes nothing: it rearranges the same numbers into a new shape.

walk.title: Reshape
walk.text: The same numbers, rearranged into the shape the next block expects.

pool.label: pooling
pool.formula: y = meanₜ xₜ, maxₜ xₜ, or x₀ (the [cls] token)
pool.prose: The positions are merged into one vector: their mean, their maximum channel by channel, or the first position alone when it is the [cls] token:
pool.unit_how: A pooling step turns a sequence into a single vector, by averaging the positions, keeping each channel's largest value, or reading the [cls] token.

walk.title: Many positions into one
walk.text: The sequence becomes one vector by the pooling the spec names: the mean over the positions, the maximum of each channel, or the [cls] token alone.

head.label: output layer
head.formula: z = w₁·{v}₁ + w₂·{v}₂ + … + w{n_sub}·{v}{n_sub} + b ; then the link
head.prose: Each of the {units} outputs of the output layer is a weighted sum of the {inputs} numbers before it plus a bias: a raw score, which the link then turns into the answer:
head.unit_how: An output unit adds up the numbers of the layer before it, each times a weight of its own, plus a bias; the link function then reads that raw sum.

walk.title: The head: raw scores
walk.text: The last layer, with one output per score the task needs. These raw numbers, the logits, are what the stepper's output step shows before the link turns them into the answer.

cumulative.formula: s = w·h ; θ₀ = first, θⱼ = θⱼ₋₁ − softplus(gapⱼ₋₁) ; zⱼ = s + θⱼ
cumulative.prose: For ordered classes the head computes one shared score s, a weighted sum of the {inputs} numbers before it, and adds to it each of {units} ordered thresholds; the thresholds only go down, so the chance of lying above each one goes down too:
cumulative.unit_how: The ordinal head scores the {row.one} once and compares that score with a ladder of learned thresholds, one per boundary between neighbouring classes.

walk.title: The head for ordered classes
walk.text: One shared score and a ladder of thresholds that can only go down: each threshold is the one before it minus a positive gap. So the chance of lying above a boundary shrinks from one boundary to the next, and every class keeps a probability of at least zero.

decoder.label: decoder
decoder.prose: The decoder is a run of dense layers, its widths the encoder's reversed, that rebuilds {units} numbers from the compressed code:
decoder.unit_how: A decoder unit works like any dense unit; together the decoder layers rebuild the inputs from the compressed code the encoder produced.

walk.title: The decoder
walk.text: Dense layers whose widths mirror the encoder's, ending on as many numbers as the inputs it rebuilds. How far the rebuilt numbers lie from the real ones is what the reconstruction error measures.

reparameterize.label: latent code
reparameterize.formula: μ, log σ² = split(h) ; answering: z = μ ; training: z = μ + σ ⊙ ε
reparameterize.prose: The layer before it produced two halves, the mean μ and the log-variance log σ² of a code of {z} numbers. While answering the code is the mean itself; only in training was noise drawn around it:
reparameterize.unit_how: A latent unit describes a range rather than a point: a mean and a spread. Training draws the code from that range; answering takes the mean, so the same {row.one} always gets the same answer.

walk.title: The latent code
walk.text: The input is split into a mean and a log-variance for each of the code's numbers. In training the code is drawn around the mean with that spread, and its divergence from a standard normal is added to the loss; while answering, the code is the mean and nothing is drawn.

gcn_conv.label: graph convolution
gcn_conv.formula: h′ᵢ = Σ_(j ∈ N̂(i)) cⱼᵢ · W·hⱼ + b ; cⱼᵢ = wⱼᵢ / √(d̂ⱼ·d̂ᵢ) (sym) or wⱼᵢ / d̂ᵢ (rw)
gcn_conv.prose: Each {node.one} gathers the projected vectors W·h of its neighbours, and its own when the layer adds self loops, each weighed by its {edge.one} and scaled down by how connected the two ends are, and adds its bias:
gcn_conv.unit_how: A graph convolution lets each {node.one} average what its neighbours carry, weighed by the {edge.many} and by how connected each neighbour is, through one shared set of weights.

walk.title: A graph convolution
walk.text: Every {node.one} projects its vector with the same weights; then each {node.one} sums the projections of its neighbours, and its own with self loops, each scaled by the {edge.one} weight and by the degrees at both ends, and adds a bias. The coefficients are recomputed from the {edge.many}, so the explanation of a {node.one} names each neighbour's share.

sage_conv.label: GraphSAGE convolution
sage_conv.formula: h′ᵢ = W_n·agg_(j ∈ N(i)) (wⱼᵢ·hⱼ) + b + W_r·hᵢ ; agg = mean, max or sum ; optionally h′ᵢ ← h′ᵢ / ‖h′ᵢ‖
sage_conv.prose: Each {node.one} aggregates its neighbours' vectors, each weighed by its {edge.one}, projects the aggregate with one set of weights and, unless the root weight is off, its own vector with another, and adds the two:
sage_conv.unit_how: A GraphSAGE layer keeps a {node.one}'s own vector apart from its neighbourhood: one set of weights reads the {node.one} itself, another reads the aggregate of its neighbours.

walk.title: A GraphSAGE convolution
walk.text: The neighbours' vectors are aggregated by mean, maximum or sum, projected, and added to the {node.one}'s own projected vector; an optional normalisation then scales each result to unit length.

gat_conv.label: graph attention layer
gat_conv.formula: eⱼᵢ = LeakyReLU(a_srcᵀ·W·hⱼ + a_dstᵀ·W·hᵢ) ; αⱼᵢ = softmax of eⱼᵢ over the edges into i ; h′ᵢ = ‖_heads Σⱼ αⱼᵢ·wⱼᵢ·W·hⱼ + b (the heads' mean when concat is off)
gat_conv.prose: Each of the {heads} heads scores every {edge.one} into a {node.one} from the projected vectors at its two ends, bent by a LeakyReLU of slope {slope}, turns the scores into weights with a softmax over the {node.one}'s incoming {edge.many}, and sums the neighbours' projected vectors with those weights:
gat_conv.unit_how: A graph attention layer lets each {node.one} decide how much to listen to each neighbour: it scores every incoming {edge.one}, turns the scores into weights, and takes the weighted mix of the neighbours.

walk.title: Graph attention
walk.text: Each head projects the vectors, scores every {edge.one} from its two ends, and normalises the scores over the {edge.many} into each {node.one}; the {edge.one} weight multiplies the attention after the softmax. The heads' results are laid side by side, or averaged when concat is off.

gin_conv.label: GIN convolution
gin_conv.formula: h′ᵢ = MLP((1 + ε)·hᵢ + Σ_(j ∈ N(i)) wⱼᵢ·hⱼ)
gin_conv.prose: Each {node.one} adds up its neighbours' vectors, each weighed by its {edge.one}, adds its own vector scaled by one plus ε = {eps}, and passes the sum through a small network of dense layers with ReLU between them:
gin_conv.unit_how: A GIN layer sums a {node.one}'s neighbourhood without averaging it away, then lets a small network of dense layers read that sum.

walk.title: A GIN convolution
walk.text: The sum of the neighbours plus the {node.one}'s own vector, scaled by one plus ε, goes through a small multi-layer network; ε is learned or fixed, as the spec says.

graph_pool.label: graph readout
graph_pool.formula: h_G = Σ_(i ∈ G) hᵢ, their mean, or their maximum
graph_pool.prose: All the {node.many} of one {graph.one} are merged into one vector: the sum, the mean or the maximum of their vectors, channel by channel:
graph_pool.unit_how: A readout turns a whole {graph.one} into one vector by summing, averaging or taking the maximum over its {node.many}, so the head can answer for the {graph.one}.

walk.title: The graph readout
walk.text: Every {node.one} of a {graph.one} contributes to one vector by the readout the spec names; after it the network reads {graph.many}, not {node.many}.

edge_dropout.label: edge dropout
edge_dropout.formula: training: each edge kept with probability 1 − p ; answering: every edge kept
edge_dropout.prose: While the network trained, each {edge.one} was dropped with probability p = {p:pct} before the graph layers read the graph. While it answers every {edge.one} is kept.
edge_dropout.unit_how: Edge dropout only acts in training, where it hides a random share of the {edge.many} so that no {node.one} leans on a single neighbour; while answering the graph is used whole.

walk.title: Edge dropout, off while answering
walk.text: In training a random share of the {edge.many} is hidden from the graph layers at each step. While answering the predictor runs in evaluation mode and every {edge.one} counts.

custom.label: custom block
custom.formula: y = f(x) — user code, unverified; shapes only
custom.prose: This block is user code the chain did not write: its output has {units} numbers, and the page shows its shape but cannot recompute it.
custom.unit_how: A custom block runs code supplied with the spec; the chain checks only the shape of what it produces.

walk.title: A custom block
walk.text: User code copied into the package beside the generated blocks. The compiler ran it once on a batch of the declared shape; nothing else about it is verified, and the page marks it so.

none.name: identity
none.bend: passes the sum through unchanged: the layer stays a plain weighted sum

relu.name: ReLU
relu.bend: passes positive evidence unchanged and cuts negative evidence to zero

gelu.name: GELU
gelu.formula: a = z·Φ(z), Φ the standard normal distribution function (the erf form)
gelu.bend: passes positive evidence almost unchanged and squashes negative evidence to about zero

silu.name: SiLU
silu.bend: passes positive evidence almost unchanged, dips a little below zero for small negative sums and brings large negative ones back to about zero

tanh.name: tanh
tanh.bend: squeezes every sum into the range between minus one and one, keeping its sign

sigmoid.name: sigmoid
sigmoid.bend: squeezes every sum into the range between zero and one: large negative sums go to about zero, large positive ones to about one

leaky_relu.name: Leaky ReLU
leaky_relu.bend: passes positive evidence unchanged and shrinks negative evidence to {slope} times its value

softmax.prose: Softmax then turns the raw scores into probabilities: each one's exponential, over the sum of them all.
softmax.answer: the class with the highest probability is the answer

walk.title: Scores to probabilities
walk.text: Softmax, applied once: e raised to each raw score, divided by their sum. The probabilities add up to one, and the largest score keeps the largest share.

sigmoid.prose: The logistic function then turns the raw score into the probability of the positive class.
sigmoid.answer: the positive class when its probability reaches the threshold, the other class otherwise

walk.title: A raw score to a probability
walk.text: The logistic function squeezes the raw score into a probability between zero and one; the answer is the positive class when it reaches the threshold the evaluation chose.

sigmoid_each.formula: pₖ = σ(zₖ), each label on its own
sigmoid_each.prose: Each label's raw score then goes through the logistic function on its own.
sigmoid_each.answer: every label whose probability reaches its threshold

walk.title: One probability per label
walk.text: Each label's raw score goes through the logistic function on its own; every label whose probability reaches its threshold is in the answer, so a {row.one} may carry several labels or none.

identity.formula: ŷ = z (then the inverse of the target's transform, when the recipe has one)
identity.prose: The raw number is the answer, put back in the target's own units when the recipe transformed the target.

walk.title: The raw number is the answer
walk.text: For a value the head's number is the answer itself; when the recipe transformed the target, the inverse of that transform puts it back in the target's own units.

cumulative.formula: P(y > j) = σ(zⱼ) ; p₀ = 1 − σ(z₀), pⱼ = σ(zⱼ₋₁) − σ(zⱼ), p_(K−1) = σ(z_(K−2))
cumulative.prose: Each raw number then becomes the probability that the answer lies above one boundary between neighbouring classes; the differences between neighbouring boundaries give each class its probability.
cumulative.answer: the class reached by counting the boundaries the service's decision rule says the {row.one} passes

walk.title: Thresholds to an ordered class
walk.text: Each of the head's numbers says how likely the answer lies above one boundary of the ordered classes; counting the boundaries passed gives the class, and the differences between neighbouring ones give each class its probability.

reconstruction.prose: The error is the mean squared distance between the rebuilt numbers and the real ones, plus a cross-entropy term for each nominal {feature.one}.
reconstruction.answer: the reconstruction error; an anomaly lane flags the {row.one} when it reaches the threshold

walk.title: The rebuilt {row.one} and its error
walk.text: The head rebuilds the inputs it was given; the answer is how far the rebuilt numbers lie from the real ones, and in an anomaly lane a {row.one} is flagged when that error reaches the threshold.

distance.prose: The score is the squared distance between the network's point for this {row.one} and the centre fitted in training.
distance.answer: the distance; the {row.one} is flagged when it reaches the threshold

walk.title: Distance from the centre
walk.text: The network maps the {row.one} to a point; the answer is its squared distance from the centre fitted in training, and a {row.one} is flagged when that distance reaches the threshold.

horizon.formula: ŷ_(t+h) = z_h, h = 1 … H (quantile loss: z_(h,q))
horizon.prose: Each raw number is the forecast for one step ahead, in order.
horizon.answer: one value per step ahead, or a band of quantiles under a quantile loss

walk.title: One value per step ahead
walk.text: Each of the head's numbers is the forecast for one step ahead, in order; under a quantile loss each step ahead gets a band of quantiles instead of a single value.

walk_fixed.title: Start-up: the composition root
walk_fixed.text: The one function that picks the concrete pieces and wires them. It checks the data files against the manifest, reads the spec, loads the weights through the store, and hands the network and the preprocessing to the predictor. Nothing further down imports its neighbours; each piece is given what it needs, here.

walk_fixed.title: The weights, trusted by digest
walk_fixed.text: The store recomputes the digest of the weights inside the file and refuses to load them if it differs from the one the evaluation recorded, so the network that answers is the one that was measured. Then it builds the network from the spec and pours the weights in.

walk_fixed.title: The network, built from its spec
walk_fixed.text: Nothing about the layers is written out by hand: the builder reads the spec shipped beside the code, block by block, and instantiates each one. The drawing on the network page is read from the same modules, so the two cannot disagree.

walk_fixed.title: The forward pass
walk_fixed.text: The blocks applied in the order the spec lists them, each one reading what the one before it produced, or the nominal inputs or the graph it needs. Nothing else happens between the shaped numbers and the head's raw scores.

walk_fixed.title: Raw scores to the answer
walk_fixed.text: The link function of the task, applied once: it turns the head's raw scores into the answer, here and nowhere else, the same way the evaluation did.

walk_fixed.title: A raw {row.one}, shaped
walk_fixed.text: Before any of that, the recipe the data stage fitted on the training part is replayed with the parameters stored beside it — these are the x₁ … xₙ of the stepper's first step. This file was generated from the recipe, not written by hand, so it cannot drift from what the network was trained on.

walk_fixed.title: Answering a request
walk_fixed.text: The predictor assembles the shaped table into the batch the network reads, puts the network in evaluation mode, switches gradients off, and reads the head's output through the same readout the evaluation used.

walk_fixed.title: Where the explanation comes from
walk_fixed.text: Not a second model. The same forward pass runs with hooks, attached once when the service starts, that only read each stage's output; one backward pass from the explained output then gives, for each of them, how far it would move that output — its gradient. No weight is changed. The drawings weigh each edge by weight × activation × gradient; the families' bars are gradient × input.

walk_fixed.title: The HTTP route
walk_fixed.text: The request is checked against the input contract before any {row.one} reaches the predictor — a malformed {row.one} is refused with a report that names the column — and every answer carries the model's version, the digest of the weights that produced it.
